_disclaimer: This file contains entirely fabricated, illustrative audience segment data created for demonstration and development purposes only. It does not represent real Are Media inventory, actual audience sizes, genuine CPM rates, or any proprietary Are Media data. All figures — reach, index, CPM, identity match rates — are invented for realism and should not be quoted, shared, or relied upon as factual. Are Media is a real publisher; this taxonomy is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or derived from any official Are Media product.

segments.description: Readers who regularly engage with beauty editorial content across Are Media's portfolio, including skincare guides, makeup tutorials, seasonal trend reports, and product reviews; identified through sustained multi-session browsing of beauty category pages on The Australian Women's Weekly and marie claire digital properties over a 60-day window.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~42% with ARE_FAH_001 (Fashion Content Consumers) — avoid stacking without frequency caps. Peaks slightly during autumn and spring trend cycles (Mar–Apr, Sep–Oct). Highest-reach beauty entry point on the network; use as prospecting layer before investing in narrower segments.

segments.description: Women who regularly consume interior design inspiration, home styling tips, renovation ideas, and homewares editorial across Australian House & Garden and Better Homes & Gardens digital platforms; behaviour includes high page depth on room-by-room feature guides and click-through on product spotlight modules.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~38% with ARE_HOM_002 (Home Renovation Planners) and ~22% with ARE_FIN_004 (Property Researchers). Engagement peaks January–March post-summer renovation season. Contextual signal only — lower identity match rate than behavioural segments; supplement with DSP-onboarded activation for addressable reach.

segments.description: Women who actively search for, read, and save recipes, meal planning guides, and cooking inspiration across Better Homes & Gardens and The Australian Women's Weekly food sections; characterised by repeated visits to recipe index pages, use of save and bookmark functionality, and high engagement with step-by-step cooking content.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~45% with ARE_FOO_002 (Home Entertaining) — treat as prospecting layer for the entertaining segment. Recency set to 30 days as food intent signals decay quickly. Volume spikes pre-Easter (Mar) and pre-Christmas (Nov–Dec). Highest-reach food segment on network.

segments.description: Engaged readers of health editorial covering nutrition, fitness advice, mental wellbeing, women's health topics, and preventive care across The Australian Women's Weekly and marie claire; segment qualifies users who consume three or more distinct health articles per month across at least two visits.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~55% with ARE_HEA_003 (Premium Wellness Buyers) when stacked — reduce impressions budget by at least 30% to avoid frequency fatigue. Consistent year-round with a measurable spike in January (New Year wellness resolutions). Broad health intent; use narrower segments for pharma, supplement, or fitness product activations requiring higher purchase propensity.

segments.description: Women who regularly browse fashion editorial, seasonal trend reports, style guides, and designer coverage across ELLE and marie claire Australia; behaviour encompasses trend landing pages, fashion week recap content, and style advice articles with high session frequency and return visit patterns.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~42% with ARE_BEA_001 (Beauty Enthusiasts Broad) and ~28% with ARE_FAH_002 (Luxury Fashion Aspirants). Peaks during Australian Fashion Week (May) and Spring Racing season (Oct–Nov). Entry-level fashion segment; use as prospecting base before investing in purchase-intent tiers.

segments.description: Mothers and primary caregivers across all stages of parenting — from pregnancy through to secondary school — who engage with parenting advice, child development content, family lifestyle articles, and product guides on Bounty Parents and The Australian Women's Weekly; the broadest parenting audience on the Are Media network.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~80% with ARE_PAR_002 (New Parents 0–2yrs) when stacked — treat these as additive reach tiers, not independent buys; stacking will over-invest against new parents disproportionately. Highest-volume audience in the parenting vertical. Back-to-school periods (late Jan, late Jul) show strong engagement lifts.

segments.description: Women consuming destination guides, holiday inspiration articles, travel listicles, and accommodation features across The Australian Women's Weekly and ELLE Australia travel sections; includes users who click through to flight and hotel partner content, signalling early-stage travel planning behaviour.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~50% with ARE_TRV_002 (Domestic Travel Planners). Recency extended to 90 days reflecting longer travel planning cycles. Broad travel inspiration intent — use ARE_TRV_002 or ARE_TRV_003 for stronger in-market purchase signals. Lowest CPM in the travel vertical; suitable for awareness-phase travel campaigns.

segments.description: Women actively reading personal finance editorial covering budgeting, cost-of-living tips, savings strategies, and financial wellness across The Australian Women's Weekly and New Idea; characterised by engagement with practical money management articles, household budgeting guides, and value-for-money product content.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~35% with ARE_FIN_002 (Super & Investment Researchers). Skews toward value-conscious, mainstream readers; complement with ARE_FIN_003 for premium finance messaging reaching higher-income women. EOFY period (May–Jun) shows measurable engagement lift.

segments.description: Women who demonstrate consistent, repeated engagement with skincare content including product comparison articles, step-by-step routine how-to guides, ingredient explainers, and dermatologist Q&As across ELLE and marie claire; distinguished from casual beauty browsers by return visits specifically targeting skincare sub-categories and engagement with regimen-building content.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~70% with ARE_BEA_004 (Prestige Skincare Purchasers) — stacking these two segments will significantly over-invest against the same high-value cohort. Use one or the other depending on message sophistication and price point. Strong year-round performance with slight dips over Christmas holidays.

segments.description: Readers who regularly consume hair care tutorials, seasonal colour trend guides, styling product reviews, salon services advice, and hair health content on ELLE and marie claire Australia; segment signals include high engagement with before-and-after gallery content, click-through on haircare product recommendation modules, and repeat visits to colour and treatment sub-sections.
segments.notes: Limited overlap with other beauty segments (~20% shared with ARE_BEA_001). Delivers well in winter months when hair care and treatment interest increases (Jun–Aug). Effective for professional salon brands, colourant products, and premium shampoo and treatment lines. Can be stacked with ARE_BEA_002 with manageable (~20%) duplication.

segments.description: Women actively researching home improvement projects including kitchen and bathroom renovations, garden landscaping, structural extensions, and interior upgrades; identified by sustained multi-session engagement with project cost guides, before-and-after renovation features, tradie advice articles, and product specification content on Australian House & Garden and Better Homes & Gardens.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~60% with ARE_HOM_003 (Luxury Home Renovation Spenders) — do not stack without suppression list. Peaks strongly in spring (Sep–Nov) and immediately post-summer (Feb–Mar). Effective for hardware retailers, kitchen and bath brands, appliance manufacturers, and renovation finance products.

segments.description: Women who plan and host dinner parties, large family gatherings, and social entertaining occasions at home, evidenced by engagement with menu planning content, table styling guides, wine and cocktail pairing articles, and seasonal entertaining features on Better Homes & Gardens and The Australian Women's Weekly; a more socially motivated food audience than recipe browsers.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~45% with ARE_FOO_001 (Recipe Seekers). Strong seasonal peaks: Christmas (Dec), Easter (Mar–Apr), and long weekend clusters throughout the year. Recommended for alcohol and wine brands, premium kitchenware, specialty food retailers, and tableware. Merges effectively with ARE_FOO_003 during Christmas activation windows.

segments.description: Women engaged with exercise content, structured workout plans, gym equipment reviews, running and walking guides, yoga and pilates content, and sports nutrition advice across marie claire and The Australian Women's Weekly; characterised by regular visits to fitness sub-sections and high engagement with activewear and wearable technology product editorials.
segments.notes: Peaks January–February (New Year fitness resolutions) and September–October (pre-summer body prep). Effective for activewear brands, gym memberships, nutrition supplements, wearable tech, and running footwear. Overlaps ~25% with ARE_HEA_003 (Premium Wellness) — manageable duplication for most plans.

segments.description: Women actively reading content about stress management, anxiety reduction, sleep quality improvement, mindfulness practices, and emotional wellbeing on marie claire and The Australian Women's Weekly; segment includes readers who engage with therapist-authored content, self-care guides, and mental health awareness editorial across sustained return visits.
segments.notes: Sensitive category — verify brand suitability before activation; pharmaceutical and alcohol brands should apply additional editorial care and seek pre-clearance. Overlaps ~25% with ARE_HEA_001 (Health Broad). Consistent year-round engagement with a small spike in late January (post-holiday re-entry stress). Suitable for meditation apps, sleep brands, herbal wellness, and allied health services.

segments.description: Women who regularly consume luxury fashion editorial, designer profile features, runway coverage, and aspirational accessory content on ELLE Australia; identified by high session depth on designer brand pages, engagement with 'investment piece' editorial, and click-through on luxury accessories and handbag guides — the aspiration signal that precedes purchase intent in the luxury fashion funnel.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~60% with ARE_FAH_003 (Designer Fashion Buyers) — use purchase intent signals to separate aspirants from confirmed in-market buyers and avoid wasted frequency. Peaks during Australian Fashion Week (May) and pre-Christmas gifting season (Nov–Dec). Brand safety pre-qualification recommended for luxury clients.

segments.description: Mothers and caregivers of infants and toddlers up to 24 months, engaging with newborn care advice, sleep training guidance, breastfeeding and formula support, developmental milestone content, and baby product reviews on Bounty Parents; segment is anchored by declared parenting stage data collected at Bounty Parents registration, making it the highest-confidence parenting audience on the network.
segments.notes: Declared data from Bounty Parents registration — highest identity match rate in the parenting vertical. Overlaps ~80% with ARE_PAR_001 (Parents Broad) when stacked. Rolling audience tied to Australian birth rate (~300k/year); suppress users after 24 months using declared child DOB from registration data. Best-in-class for baby formula, pram, nappy, and infant care brands.

segments.description: Women actively planning Australian domestic holidays, weekend getaways, and family road trips, evidenced by engagement with state-by-state destination guides, regional accommodation reviews, family-friendly activity content, and driving itinerary features on The Australian Women's Weekly and Better Homes & Gardens travel sections; a stronger purchase intent signal than the broader travel inspiration segment.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~50% with ARE_TRV_001 (Travel Inspiration Browsers) — stacking inflates reach without proportional incremental audience. Strongest delivery around school holiday windows (Jan, late Mar–Apr, early Jul, mid Sep–Oct). Tourism boards, domestic airlines, caravan and camping brands, and regional hotel groups perform well.

segments.description: Women actively researching superannuation fund options, investment strategies, managed funds, share portfolios, and retirement planning on The Australian Women's Weekly financial wellness section; includes readers who engage with 'women and money' editorial, gender super gap explainers, and fund comparison guides — a segment reflecting growing female financial self-advocacy.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~35% with ARE_FIN_001 (Personal Finance Readers) and ~40% with ARE_FIN_003 (HNW Women Investors). AFSL compliance required for all investment product advertising — advertisers must pre-clear creative before activation. End-of-financial-year spike (May–Jun) is the strongest planning window for this segment.

segments.description: Women with demonstrated purchase behaviour toward prestige skincare brands including targeted serums, high-SPF moisturisers, retinol treatments, vitamin C formulations, and professional-grade anti-ageing products priced above $80 AUD per unit; identified through engagement with clinical skincare ingredient deep-dives, luxury brand editorial coverage, and 'is it worth the spend' review features on ELLE and marie claire.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~70% with ARE_BEA_002 (Skincare Routine Builders) — do not stack; choose one based on price point of advertised product. High CPM is justified by confirmed spend propensity at premium price points. Suitable for La Mer, Chanel Beauté, SkinCeuticals, Medik8, and comparable prestige brands. Stacking with ARE_FAH_003 adds ~20% duplication — manageable but apply a weekly frequency cap of 3.

segments.description: Women with active purchase signals for luxury and designer fashion, accessories, and footwear at price points above $500 AUD, identified through engagement with 'shop now' shoppable editorial units on ELLE Australia, click-through to luxury retail partner destinations, and declared luxury purchasing behaviour in Are Media reader surveys — the highest-value fashion audience on the network.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~60% with ARE_FAH_002 (Luxury Fashion Aspirants). Smallest addressable luxury fashion audience on the network — stacking with ARE_BEA_004, ARE_TRV_003, or ARE_FIN_003 without frequency caps risks rapid saturation (estimated total unduplicated addressable audience across all three: ~65k). Pre-qualify creative for luxury brand safety compliance.

segments.description: Women with high household income and active engagement with wealth management, share portfolio management, property investment, and private banking content; identified through declared income brackets ($200k+ household) in Are Media reader registration, sustained engagement with premium investment editorial on ELLE Australia, and repeat visits to wealth-building and financial independence content.
segments.notes: AFSL compliance required for all financial product creative. Overlaps ~40% with ARE_FIN_002 (Super & Investment). Very small pool — stacking with ARE_FAH_003 or ARE_TRV_003 risks rapid frequency overload; enforce a hard cap of 3 impressions per user per week. Best suited to private banking, wealth management, premium property, and family office-adjacent brands.

segments.description: Women actively planning or mid-way through high-budget home renovation or new-build projects valued above $100,000 AUD, identified through declared project value and stage in reader surveys, sustained engagement with architect and interior designer profiles, and deep reading of luxury kitchen, bathroom, and landscape features on Australian House & Garden.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~60% with ARE_HOM_002 (Home Renovation Planners) — do not stack; treat as premium tier of the renovation audience. Spring activation (Sep–Nov) is strongest; buyers at this decision level typically take 6–12 months from research to final purchase. Effective for premium appliance, Miele, Sub-Zero, Terzetto, Porcelanosa, and bespoke architectural lighting brands.

segments.description: Women with a demonstrated preference for luxury travel experiences including business and first class flights, five-star resort accommodation, private guided tours, and high-end cruise itineraries; identified through declared travel spend (above $10,000 AUD per trip) in reader surveys, engagement with luxury travel editorial on ELLE Australia, and click-through to premium airline and resort partner content.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~40% with ARE_FIN_003 and ~30% with ARE_FAH_003 — a three-way stack will exhaust this audience within days; mandatory frequency cap of 3/week. Recency 90 days reflects extended luxury travel planning cycles (often 6+ months ahead of departure). Peak intent aligns with high-season international travel: Dec–Jan and Jun–Jul.

segments.description: Mothers of children aged 0–3 years who actively research and purchase premium baby and toddler products including prams priced above $800, organic nursery furniture, natural and certified-organic baby skincare, and premium nutrition brands; identified through declared purchase history on Bounty Parents and sustained engagement with premium product editorial and 'worth the investment' gear guides.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~75% with ARE_PAR_002 (New Parents 0–2yrs) — treat as a premium sub-tier, not a separate buy; use for brands targeting the upper quartile of new parent spend. Rolling audience tied to birth cohorts; suppress after child turns 3 using declared DOB. Effective for Bugaboo, Ergobaby, Nûk, Wotnot, and Joonya brand equivalents.

segments.description: Women actively purchasing or demonstrably in-market for premium vitamins, marine collagen, probiotics and prebiotics, adaptogens, magnesium supplements, and premium wellness products; evidenced by engagement with supplement comparison guides, clinical nutrition deep-dives, and 'worth buying' wellness roundups on marie claire and The Australian Women's Weekly.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~55% with ARE_HEA_001 (Health Broad) — do not stack without suppression list. TGA-compliant creative mandatory for supplement brands; advertisers must confirm therapeutic claim compliance before activation. Peaks January (New Year wellness) and June–July (winter immune season). Suitable for Vida Glow, JSHealth, The Beauty Chef, and comparable premium supplement brands.

segments.description: Women actively planning Christmas celebrations including festive menus, gift shopping and wrapping guides, table decoration inspiration, hamper curation, and holiday hosting logistics; identified through engagement with Christmas-specific editorial content across Better Homes & Gardens, The Australian Women's Weekly, and New Idea in the October–December window.
segments.notes: SEASONAL — activates October 1 to December 31 only; segment data is not meaningful outside this window. Overlaps heavily with ARE_FOO_001 (~60%) and ARE_FOO_002 (~55%) during peak season — avoid triple stacking in November–December. Book inventory by September 30 to secure premium placements; the second and third weeks of December are the highest-competition period on the Are Media network.

segments.description: Parents of school-aged children actively planning family holidays during Australian school holiday periods — January summer break, Easter, July winter break, and September–October spring break; identified by measurable spikes in engagement with family travel guides, child-friendly destination content, theme park reviews, and budget-family itinerary features on Bounty Parents and The Australian Women's Weekly.
segments.notes: SEASONAL — four distinct activation windows: January, late March–April, early July, and mid September–October. Reach figure reflects average across active months; peaks at approximately 450k in January. Overlaps ~50% with ARE_TRV_002 during school holiday windows — manageable if campaigns are school-holiday themed. Domestic airlines, theme parks, resort properties, and car rental brands perform strongly in this segment.

segments.description: Women actively researching and purchasing sun protection, after-sun treatment, self-tanning, and summer skin preparation products in the lead-up to and during the Australian summer; identified through engagement with SPF product comparisons, sun care routine guides, and summer beauty editorial on ELLE and marie claire in the October–February window.
segments.notes: SEASONAL — primary activation window October 1 to February 28; residual activity in March. Overlaps ~30% with ARE_HEA_001 (Health Broad) and ~25% with ARE_BEA_002 (Skincare Routine Builders). Volume peaks in October–November as purchase intent precedes the summer season — sunscreen and SPF brands should book October delivery to capture pre-season planning behaviour rather than waiting for December.

segments.description: Women motivated by the spring season to undertake home cleaning, decluttering, storage reorganisation, room refreshing, and outdoor entertaining area preparation; identified through engagement with spring cleaning checklists, storage solutions roundups, garden preparation guides, and seasonal homewares refresh editorial on Better Homes & Gardens and Australian House & Garden.
segments.notes: SEASONAL — peaks September–October; secondary activity cluster in January (post-Christmas clear-out). Overlaps ~35% with ARE_HOM_001 (Home Browsers) during activation period. Effective for cleaning product brands, storage retailers, garden centres, outdoor furniture, and premium paint. October inventory competes with ARE_FOO_003 (Christmas) and ARE_FAH_004 (Spring Racing) — plan budgets across verticals carefully to avoid bidding against own campaigns.

segments.description: Women actively planning outfits, accessories, and beauty looks for Melbourne Cup, Spring Racing Carnival events, and associated spring social occasions; identified through engagement with race day fashion guides, millinery and fascinator features, frock-shopping editorial, occasion dressing advice, and champagne entertaining content across ELLE and The Australian Women's Weekly.
segments.notes: SEASONAL — October 1 to November 15 only; audience is negligible outside this window. Overlaps ~40% with ARE_FAH_001 (Fashion Broad) and ~35% with ARE_FAH_002 (Luxury Aspirants). Effective for fashion retailers, beauty and fragrance brands, champagne and spirits, racecourse operators, and milliners. Book inventory before September 1 — premium placements sell out in the final two weeks of October.

segments.description: Mothers and caregivers of primary school-age children engaging with content covering school readiness, extracurricular activity planning, family-friendly meal ideas, children's health and nutrition, and family home management on Bounty Parents and The Australian Women's Weekly; segment captures the organised-family stage where household purchase influence is broad and category involvement spans food, education, health, and leisure.
segments.notes: Distinct from ARE_PAR_002 (0–2 years) and ARE_PAR_003 (premium baby) with low duplication (<15%). Back-to-school periods (mid-January, late July) and school term beginnings are peak engagement windows. Effective for packaged food brands, education technology, family vehicles, children's health products, and after-school activity brands.

segments.description: Women actively reading plant-based, vegetarian, and nutritionally conscious recipe content and engaging with clean eating guides, ingredient substitution tutorials, gut health nutrition articles, and health-focused food editorial on Better Homes & Gardens and marie claire; segment reflects a growing flexitarian audience who are motivated by both health outcomes and environmental concerns.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~30% with ARE_HEA_002 (Fitness & Active) and ~20% with ARE_HEA_003 (Premium Wellness). Limited seasonal variation; slight spike in January driven by healthy new year resolutions. Effective for plant-based food brands (Impossible Foods, Oatly equivalents), health food retailers, organic grocery, and vegetarian meal kit services. Fastest-growing food sub-segment on the network year-on-year.

segments.description: Women actively researching property purchase decisions, investment property opportunities, or rental market intelligence, evidenced by engagement with real estate market commentary, suburb profile guides, property styling advice ahead of sale, and mortgage and stamp duty content across The Australian Women's Weekly and Australian House & Garden.
segments.notes: Overlaps ~22% with ARE_HOM_001 (Home Browsers) and ~35% with ARE_FIN_001 (Personal Finance). AFSL and credit licence compliance required for mortgage product advertising. Segment volume is sensitive to RBA cash rate movements — monitor external signals when scheduling activation. Strong cross-category appeal for mortgage brokers, conveyancers, property platforms, and moving services.

segments.description: Women who actively seek sustainable living solutions, eco-friendly home products, energy efficiency improvements, solar and battery content, and low-waste household management strategies; identified through engagement with sustainability features, 'green home' renovation guides, ethical homewares roundups, and composting and zero-waste editorial on Better Homes & Gardens and Australian House & Garden.
segments.notes: Fastest-growing home sub-segment on the Are Media network based on year-on-year content engagement trends. Overlaps ~25% with ARE_HOM_001 (Home Browsers) and ~20% with ARE_HEA_001 (Health Broad). Effective for solar and battery brands, ethical cleaning products (Koala Eco, Resparkle equivalents), B Corp-certified homewares, and energy retailers. No strong seasonal pattern — consistent year-round growth.

segments.description: Career-focused women engaging with workwear styling guides, capsule wardrobe building content, business casual dressing advice, and office-to-event transition outfit features on ELLE and marie claire Australia; a considered purchasing audience making deliberate, higher-price-point wardrobe investments for professional contexts.
segments.notes: Minimal seasonal variation; slight dip in January and July (school holiday periods). Overlaps ~20% with ARE_FAH_001 (Fashion Broad) and ~15% with ARE_FIN_002 (Super & Investment) reflecting professional demographic crossover. Post-pandemic return-to-office trend has grown this segment materially since 2023. Effective for mid-to-premium apparel, quality footwear, structured bags, and professional watch brands.

segments.description: Women aged 40 and above actively seeking information about perimenopause, menopause, hormonal health management, bone density, sleep disruption, mood changes, and midlife wellbeing across The Australian Women's Weekly and marie claire; a fast-growing segment reflecting the mainstream editorial shift toward open, evidence-based menopause health coverage that has significantly expanded Are Media's 40+ health audience in the past two years.
segments.notes: Sensitive health category — pharmaceutical creative (including HRT brands) requires TGA compliance review before activation. Fastest-growing editorial audience on AWW digital in 2024–2025 by unique monthly reader growth. Minimal overlap with other health sub-segments (<15%) — can be safely stacked with ARE_HEA_001 or ARE_HEA_002 without meaningful duplication. Effective for HRT pharmaceutical brands, bone health supplements, quality sleep brands, and premium midlife wellness products. No strong seasonal pattern.
